screens.title: Troubleshooting Common MySQL Issues
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you'll learn a practical troubleshooting workflow for MySQL. Troubleshooting starts with careful information gathering: symptoms, when they began, and recent changes. Logs are often the fastest route to an answer — the MySQL error log and slow query log contain explicit clues about startup failures, deadlocks, and long-running queries. We'll also cover specific problems you will see in the field: connection failures and the "Too many connections" error, diagnosing slow queries with the slow query log and EXPLAIN, analyzing InnoDB deadlocks using SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS, and handling disk space exhaustion safely. Each topic includes a concrete command or example you can run in a terminal, plus a common mistake to avoid, such as blindly increasing max_connections. Throughout, safety matters: back up before making structural changes, test in staging, and prefer configuration edits backed up by a copy of my. cnf. By the end of this chapter you will have a repeatable sequence: capture evidence, inspect logs, run specific diagnostic commands, apply safe short-term fixes, and plan a long-term resolution. Consider how you'll apply this pattern the next time an alert spikes — what logs will you check first and which temporary fix will you avoid?

Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › Overview
Troubleshooting Common MySQL Issues
A safety-first, evidence-driven approach to find and fix server problems quickly without making things worse.
In this lesson
Gather logs, run diagnostic commands, apply safe fixes, and plan permanent remedies.
Why it matters
Fast, safe recovery keeps applications available and prevents data loss. The right diagnostic steps avoid costly missteps.
Explore Key Topics
Connections
Diagnose "Can't connect" and "Too many connections" using service and processlist checks.
Slow Queries
Use the slow query log and EXPLAIN to reveal missing indexes and inefficient plans.
Deadlocks & Disk
Read InnoDB status for deadlocks and free disk safely by purging logs and rotating files.
Visual Summary
Capture logs
error log, slow query log, processlist
Run diagnostics
EXPLAIN, SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS, df -h
Apply fixes safely
temporary increases, purge logs, add indexes, then plan permanent changes
Quick note
Always back up data before structural changes. Test fixes in staging first. Logs are your best friend when diagnosis is urgent.

screens.title: A systematic troubleshooting workflow
screens.narratorSegment: A reliable troubleshooting workflow prevents guesswork and accelerates resolution. Start by recording the observable symptoms: error messages, affected services, and the exact time the issue started. Next, identify recent changes: deployments, configuration edits, or OS updates — change correlation often points to a cause. Third, capture logs immediately: copy the MySQL error log and the slow query log, because they may grow or rotate. Fourth, run targeted diagnostics such as systemctl status mysqld, df -h for disk checks, SHOW PROCESSLIST to view active sessions, and SHOW GLOBAL STATUS LIKE 'Max_used_connections' to learn peaks. Fifth, apply safe temporary mitigations, for example increase max_connections temporarily to avoid immediate outages, but do not leave it permanent without addressing the root cause. Finally, plan and test a long-term fix in staging, then apply it with backups in place. A concrete example: when an application deploys a new service that opens many connections, the change log plus a spike in Max_used_connections points to a pooling issue. A common misconception is to treat temporary fixes as solutions; they buy time but can mask deeper problems. Your takeaway: a checklist and captured evidence are your best tools when diagnosing production incidents. What will you record first when an alert triggers?

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › Troubleshooting Workflow
Process Flow
1
Record symptoms & time
Capture error text and affected services. Timestamps are crucial for aligning logs.
2
Check recent changes
Deploys and config edits often cause regressions; list them before altering anything.
3
Capture logs
Copy log_error and slow query logs immediately; logs can rotate and be lost.
4
Run diagnostics
systemctl status mysqld, SHOW PROCESSLIST, df -h, SHOW GLOBAL STATUS checks reveal many causes.
5
Mitigate safely and plan fixes
Temporary fixes buy time. Test permanent changes in staging with backups ready.
Common-mistake
Blindly increasing max_connections without finding why connections spike can hide leaks and increase memory pressure.
Prefer finding the root cause. Use SET GLOBAL max_connections only as a temporary relief while you inspect connection sources and pooling behavior.
Diagnostics Cheat Sheet
Check service
systemctl status mysqld or service mysqld status to confirm process health.
Inspect processes
SHOW PROCESSLIST and SELECT * FROM sys.processlist show active and sleeping connections.
Disk and logs
df -h and du -sh /var/lib/mysql/* reveal space pressure. Copy logs before rotating.
Key Takeaway

A checklist and preserved evidence speed diagnosis and help you implement safe fixes rather than risky guesswork.

screens.title: Understanding connection errors
screens.narratorSegment: Connection failures are among the most visible MySQL problems because they immediately surface to applications and users. A "Can't connect to MySQL server" symptom can come from several causes. First, the server process might not be running; verify with systemctl status mysqld or the service command. Second, network issues such as firewall rules or port misconfiguration can block access; a quick telnet to the host and port checks basic TCP connectivity. Third, authentication and privileges may prevent access for a given user and host. Finally, resource exhaustion like too many open files or sockets can stop new connections. A concrete example: if systemctl shows the server is active but telnet to port 3306 times out, the network or firewall is likely the cause, not credentials. A common misconception is to assume a permissions problem when the server is down or the port is closed; always confirm the server and network first. Your verification steps: confirm mysqld is running, test TCP connectivity, then check MySQL grants and error log entries for authentication failures. Closing question: when you see a connection error, which of those three checks will you run in what order and why?

keyIdea.title: Verify service, network, then credentials
keyIdea.text: Always confirm mysqld is running and network reachability before investigating user privileges or application-level issues.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › Connection Errors
Definition & verification steps
  • Confirm mysqld is running using systemctl or service status commands.
  • Verify TCP reachability with telnet hostname port or a simple socket check.
  • Check error log for authentication or startup messages tied to the timestamp.
Example command checks
systemctl status mysqld
# or
service mysqld status

# Test network reachability
telnet db-host.example.com 3306
Concrete example
An application reports connection failures after a deploy. systemctl shows mysqld active, but telnet times out. The deploy changed firewall rules. Reopening the port restored connections. The error log showed no authentication failures, which helped rule out grants as the cause.
Pro tip
Check service and network reachability before making user or privilege changes. That reduces unnecessary permission edits.
Key Takeaway

Confirm server process and TCP connectivity first; then analyze logs and grants for authentication issues.

screens.title: "Too many connections" and max_connections
screens.narratorSegment: The "Too many connections" error (ERROR 1040) indicates the server has reached its configured max_connections limit. This can be a capacity problem or an application issue. Start diagnosis by checking SHOW GLOBAL STATUS LIKE 'Max_used_connections'; to see the peak concurrent connections historically. If Max_used_connections rarely approaches max_connections, then occasional spikes may be transient, and a temporary increase can help while you investigate. Use SHOW PROCESSLIST or sys. processlist to see active connections and identify many sleeping connections or long-running queries. A concrete example: an application that fails to close connections properly will accumulate many sleeping connections until the limit is reached. A common misconception is that raising max_connections always solves the problem; raising it can increase server memory usage and delay discovery of leaks. The correct long-term solution is often application-side: introduce or tune connection pooling so connections are reused and closed promptly. As a diagnostic step, you can SET GLOBAL max_connections = 200 temporarily, but plan to identify and fix the root cause. What would you look for in the process list to decide between a temporary increase and an application fix?

keyIdea.title: Temporary relief vs root cause
keyIdea.text: Use Max_used_connections and processlist to decide whether to raise max_connections temporarily or fix connection management in the application.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › Too Many Connections
Quick diagnostics
SHOW GLOBAL STATUS LIKE 'Max_used_connections';
SHOW GLOBAL VARIABLES LIKE 'max_connections';
SHOW PROCESSLIST;
Look for many 'Sleep' entries or many connections from the same host or user. Long-running queries indicate resource contention rather than a pool leak.
Temporary action
SET GLOBAL max_connections = 200; only as a short-term relief while you identify leaks or pooling misconfigurations.
Concrete example
If processlist shows hundreds of sleeping connections created shortly after a deploy, check the application connection handling. In many frameworks misconfiguration causes new connections for each request instead of reusing a pool.
Common-mistake
Raising max_connections without considering memory cost can exhaust RAM and cause more severe failures.
Key Takeaway

Use processlist and Max_used_connections to decide between temporary relief and a code fix. Root cause is usually pooling or leaks.

screens.title: Using SHOW PROCESSLIST and sys.processlist
screens.narratorSegment: SHOW PROCESSLIST and the sys. processlist view are indispensable for seeing who is connected and what they are doing. Processlist rows show the connection id, user, host, command, time, and Info field with the query text. Start by ordering output by Time to find long-running queries and by Command to find many Sleep entries. A concrete example: SELECT * FROM sys. processlist WHERE command!= 'Sleep' ORDER BY TIME DESC; highlights active queries consuming resources. When you see long-running statements holding connections, examine their query text and EXPLAIN them. Use KILL only for queries you are confident are safe to terminate, and avoid killing transactions mid-write without understanding potential rollback costs. A common misconception is to mass-kill sleeping connections to free slots; sleeping connections often belong to connection pools that will reopen and might mask the leak without fixing the pooling logic. Closing question: when you see many sleeping connections from one host, what is the likely application-level cause and what metric will you monitor after fixing it? Using SHOW PROCESSLIST and sys.processlist means filter by command and time to identify active work and idle connections; kill with care and investigate pooling behavior for many sleeps.. In practical terms, find idle connections, long-running queries, and candidates for kill. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › Processlist Diagnostics
Key commands
SHOW PROCESSLIST;
-- or using sys schema
SELECT * FROM sys.processlist WHERE command != 'Sleep' ORDER BY TIME DESC;
Look for repeated hosts or users, and for queries with very large Time values or Info containing slow statements.
Example output to inspect
If many sleeps come from the application server pool, the application likely fails to reuse connections. If many long-running SELECTs appear, optimize queries or add indexes.
When to KILL
  • Kill queries that are blocked or stuck and known to be safe to stop.
  • Avoid killing transactions involved in multi-statement writes unless you understand rollback effects.
  • Document killed thread IDs and reasons to correlate with application behavior.
Key Takeaway

Use processlist to triage. Prefer fixing pooling and query performance rather than repeatedly killing sleeping connections.

screens.title: Diagnosing slow queries with the slow query log
screens.narratorSegment: The slow query log records queries that exceed a configured execution time and is central to finding recurring performance problems. Enable slow query logging by setting slow_query_log = 1, long_query_time = 1, and specifying slow_query_log_file in my. cnf, then restart if necessary. With the log enabled, you will capture queries that are candidates for optimization. Tools like mysqldumpslow or pt-query-digest parse the log and surface the most frequent or slowest queries, which helps prioritize work. A concrete example from the hands-on activity: selecting from a large users table without an index on email produces a high execution time entry in the slow log. Use EXPLAIN on that query to see type = ALL and a large rows value; that indicates a full table scan. A common misconception is to assume a single slow query is the only problem; often a family of similar queries will dominate. After identifying the offenders, add targeted indexes or rewrite queries, then monitor the slow log again to confirm improvement. Which query will you check first in your application's slow log? Diagnosing slow queries with the slow query log means enable the slow query log, parse it for frequent offenders, then use explain to prioritize indexing and rewrites.. In practical terms, enable and analyze the slow query log to find frequent offenders. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › Slow Query Log
Enable slow query logging
# my.cnf
slow_query_log = 1
long_query_time = 1
slow_query_log_file = /var/log/mysql/mysql-slow.log
After enabling, use mysqldumpslow or pt-query-digest to summarize and rank queries by frequency or time.
Concrete example
A query searching users by email without an index shows up repeatedly. The slow log shows the execution time and query text, which you then EXPLAIN to determine a full table scan.
Key Takeaway

Use the slow query log to find recurring cost-heavy queries and prioritize fixes with EXPLAIN and indexing.

screens.title: Using EXPLAIN and adding indexes
screens.narratorSegment: EXPLAIN shows how MySQL plans to execute a SELECT, helping you find full table scans and other inefficiencies. Look for type values like ALL, which indicate a full table scan, and Extra values such as Using filesort or Using temporary. The rows column shows the estimated number of rows examined. A concrete walkthrough: run EXPLAIN on a query that searches users by email. If EXPLAIN shows type = ALL and a large rows value, add an index on the email column with CREATE INDEX idx_email ON users (email);. After adding the index, EXPLAIN should change to type = ref or const and rows should be much smaller, and the actual execution time will drop. A misconception is to add indexes without checking selectivity or query patterns; unnecessary or duplicate indexes add write overhead. Always test index impact and prefer composite indexes that match WHERE clause ordering when queries filter by multiple columns. Closing question: after adding an index, which EXPLAIN columns will you inspect to confirm the improvement and why? Using EXPLAIN and adding indexes means use explain to identify scans and rows examined, then add targeted indexes and re-check explain to confirm reduced row estimates and better type values.. In practical terms, interpret query plans and apply indexes to reduce scans. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Use EXPLAIN to identify scans and rows examined, then add targeted indexes and re-check EXPLAIN to confirm reduced row estimates and better type values.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › EXPLAIN & Indexes
EXPLAIN example
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = 'user50000@example.com';
If the plan shows type = ALL and large rows, the query scans the whole table. Adding an index on email usually changes type to ref or const.
Index command
CREATE INDEX idx_email ON users (email);
Concrete result
After creating idx_email, EXPLAIN should show fewer estimated rows and a better type. Execution time for the query will drop and the slow log entry should disappear for that pattern.
Key Takeaway

Let EXPLAIN guide indexing. Confirm changes by re-running EXPLAIN and checking the slow query log for improvement.

screens.title: Deadlocks in InnoDB
screens.narratorSegment: A deadlock occurs when two or more transactions hold locks the others need, and neither can proceed. InnoDB detects deadlocks automatically and rolls back one transaction to resolve the stalemate. To diagnose, inspect the error log for deadlock messages and run SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS\G to view the LATEST DETECTED DEADLOCK section. That output shows the involved transactions, the locks they hold, and the S Q L statements; this is the most informative source for understanding the conflict. A concrete example: two transactions updating rows in two tables in opposite order can deadlock. A practical prevention strategy is to ensure transactions acquire locks in a consistent order, keep transactions short, and add indexes to shorten lock durations. A common misconception is that changing isolation levels always removes deadlocks; while READ COMMITTED can reduce contention compared to REPEATABLE READ, logical ordering and short transactions are more reliable. Your task after seeing deadlocks: read the InnoDB status output to identify the conflicting statements, then change transaction order or index patterns to eliminate the circular wait. What change would you make first if two transactions lock tables in opposite order?

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › InnoDB Deadlocks
Diagnose with InnoDB status
SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS\G
Read the LATEST DETECTED DEADLOCK section to see the transactions, locks held, and SQL statements that caused the deadlock.
Preventive practices
  • Acquire locks in a consistent order across transactions.
  • Keep transactions short and avoid user interaction inside transactions.
  • Add indexes to reduce lock duration by speeding queries.
Concrete example
Two transactions that update table A then table B and another that updates B then A can deadlock. Rewriting both to update A then B eliminates the circular wait.
Key Takeaway

Read the InnoDB deadlock details and change transaction ordering or indexing to prevent recurrence rather than relying on transient rollbacks.

screens.title: Disk space exhaustion and log management
screens.narratorSegment: Disk space exhaustion is a critical failure mode that can stop MySQL from writing and cause crashes. Symptoms include "No space left on device" in the error log, failed writes, and sudden server instability. Start diagnosis with df -h to find the impacted filesystem and du -sh /var/lib/mysql/* to identify large files. Binary logs, slow query logs, error logs, and large. ibd tablespaces are common culprits. A concrete remediation sequence: first, make a backup of essential data and logs. Second, purge old binary logs safely using PURGE BINARY LOGS TO 'mysql-bin.000123'; or set EXPIRE_LOGS_DAYS to limit retention. Third, rotate and compress logs to reclaim space. Fourth, consider OPTIMIZE TABLE table_name when innodb_file_per_table is enabled to free space after deletions, but understand it rebuilds the table and can be resource intensive. A common misconception is to delete files from the data directory directly; doing that can corrupt metadata or replication. Always use MySQL commands or rotate logs in cooperation with the server. Closing reflection: what is the safest first file or log you would archive to regain enough space to stabilize the server?

Diagnostic commands
df -h
du -sh /var/lib/mysql/*

Identify large tablespaces (.ibd), binary logs, or rotated logs consuming space and back them up before removal.
Safe purging
Purge binary logs with PURGE BINARY LOGS TO 'mysql-bin.000123'; after confirming backups and replication safety.
Concrete example
A server ran out of space due to accumulated binary logs. After backing up and purging old binary logs and restarting, writes resumed. Deleting files directly from the data directory was avoided to prevent corruption.
Key Takeaway

Back up first. Use MySQL commands to purge logs. Do not delete data files directly. Plan retention to prevent recurrence.

screens.title: Safety measures and best practices
screens.narratorSegment: Safety is paramount when troubleshooting production databases. Before any structural change, take a recent backup and, when possible, test the change in staging. Keep a copy of my. cnf before editing configuration variables so you can revert. When you need to free space or kill processes, document your actions and reasons so you can trace outcomes. Avoid deleting files directly from the MySQL data directory; use built-in commands to purge or rotate logs. When issuing KILL on threads, understand whether they are inside transactions and whether rollbacks will take time or lock resources. Always prefer making configuration changes with a clear rollback plan and changelog entry. A concrete example: before running OPTIMIZE TABLE to reclaim space, backup the table and schedule the operation during low traffic because it rebuilds the table and can be input and output intensive. A common misconception is that immediate visible fixes in production are low risk; many such actions have cascading effects. Your closing question: what three safety checks will you run before applying a change that affects data or storage? Safety measures and best practices means always back up, stage changes, keep configuration copies, and document mitigation steps. prefer mysql commands over file deletion.. In practical terms, how to work safely during troubleshooting. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › Safety & Best Practices
Safety checklist
  1. Create or verify a recent backup and confirm restoreability.
  2. Test changes in staging and keep a copy of my.cnf before edits.
  3. Document actions and have a rollback plan for each change.
When to use KILL
Kill only threads you understand. Be aware of rollbacks and replication implications before terminating active transactions.
Concrete example
Before altering retention days for binary logs, back up recent logs, change EXPIRE_LOGS_DAYS in my.cnf, and verify replication slaves can still retrieve any necessary events.
Key Takeaway

Treat every change as reversible. Backup first, test in staging, and document a clear rollback procedure.

screens.title: Hands-on: Diagnose and resolve a slow query
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on activity walks through the chapter lab to reproduce a slow query, analyze it with EXPLAIN, add an index, and confirm improvement. First, create a sample database and a users table without an index on email. Insert a large number of rows to simulate production. Run a SELECT that filters by email and note the execution time, then check the slow query log if enabled. Next, run EXPLAIN on the same SELECT and look for type = ALL and a large rows estimate — these indicate a full table scan. Add an index with CREATE INDEX idx_email ON users (email); then re-run EXPLAIN and the SELECT. You should see the type change to ref or const and a dramatic reduction in execution time. A common misconception is to expect any index will help; the index must match the query filter. Always re-run EXPLAIN and check the slow query log to confirm the fix. After the lab, reflect on how this pattern maps to your systems: which real query would you test and what is your rollback plan if an index causes unexpected write overhead?

CREATE DATABASE troubleshooting_db;
USE troubleshooting_db;

CREATE TABLE users (
  id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,

Expected observations
Before the index: EXPLAIN shows type = ALL and high rows; query is logged as slow. After index: type becomes ref or const, rows shrink, and execution time improves.
Key Takeaway

This lab demonstrates the full cycle: reproduce, analyze, fix, and verify. Confirm fixes by re-checking logs and EXPLAIN output.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you'll learn a practical troubleshooting workflow for MySQL. Troubleshooting starts with careful information gathering: symptoms, when they began, and recent changes. Logs are often the fastest route to an answer — the MySQL error log and slow query log contain explicit clues about startup failures, deadlocks, and long-running queries. We'll also cover specific problems you will see in the field: connection failures and the "Too many connections" error, diagnosing slow queries with the slow query log and EXPLAIN, analyzing InnoDB deadlocks using SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS, and handling disk space exhaustion safely. Each topic includes a concrete command or example you can run in a terminal, plus a common mistake to avoid, such as blindly increasing max_connections. Throughout, safety matters: back up before making structural changes, test in staging, and prefer configuration edits backed up by a copy of my. cnf. By the end of this chapter you will have a repeatable sequence: capture evidence, inspect logs, run specific diagnostic commands, apply safe short-term fixes, and plan a long-term resolution. Consider how you'll apply this pattern the next time an alert spikes — what logs will you check first and which temporary fix will you avoid?

In this set of objectives you'll see the skills you will build and why they are important for a working DBA. First, you will learn a systematic troubleshooting approach: how to collect symptoms, identify recent changes, and capture logs that point to causes. This skill matters because a repeatable workflow saves time and prevents ad-hoc actions that can worsen outages. Second, you will diagnose and resolve connection issues such as "Can't connect" and the 1040 "Too many connections" error. We cover commands to check service status, network reachability, and the processlist, and discuss temporary versus long-term fixes. Third, you will identify and optimize slow queries using the slow query log and EXPLAIN, including when an index will likely help. This reduces latency and improves concurrency. Fourth, you will understand InnoDB deadlocks and use SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS to find the latest detected deadlock and plan changes to transaction order or indexes. Each objective includes a competency milestone so you can verify you can perform these actions in a real environment. Which objective feels most urgent for your current systems?

This second objectives slide breaks core skills into actionable sub-skills you can verify in hands-on labs. First, capturing the right logs: configure log_error, slow_query_log, and where necessary the general query log. Know where they live and how to rotate them. Second, service and network diagnostics: verify mysqld is running, use systemctl or service commands, and check network reachability with telnet — these are the first checks when you see connection failures. Third, process inspection and temporary fixes: use SHOW PROCESSLIST and sys. processlist to find idle or long-running connections, and understand when a temporary max_connections increase is acceptable versus when you must fix application pooling. Fourth, safe disk recovery: identify large binary logs or tablespaces and safely purge or archive them only after backups. Each sub-skill ties directly to a verified milestone you can run in a lab environment. Which sub-skill will you try first in your next drill?

A reliable troubleshooting workflow prevents guesswork and accelerates resolution. Start by recording the observable symptoms: error messages, affected services, and the exact time the issue started. Next, identify recent changes: deployments, configuration edits, or OS updates — change correlation often points to a cause. Third, capture logs immediately: copy the MySQL error log and the slow query log, because they may grow or rotate. Fourth, run targeted diagnostics such as systemctl status mysqld, df -h for disk checks, SHOW PROCESSLIST to view active sessions, and SHOW GLOBAL STATUS LIKE 'Max_used_connections' to learn peaks. Fifth, apply safe temporary mitigations, for example increase max_connections temporarily to avoid immediate outages, but do not leave it permanent without addressing the root cause. Finally, plan and test a long-term fix in staging, then apply it with backups in place. A concrete example: when an application deploys a new service that opens many connections, the change log plus a spike in Max_used_connections points to a pooling issue. A common misconception is to treat temporary fixes as solutions; they buy time but can mask deeper problems. Your takeaway: a checklist and captured evidence are your best tools when diagnosing production incidents. What will you record first when an alert triggers?

Connection failures are among the most visible MySQL problems because they immediately surface to applications and users. A "Can't connect to MySQL server" symptom can come from several causes. First, the server process might not be running; verify with systemctl status mysqld or the service command. Second, network issues such as firewall rules or port misconfiguration can block access; a quick telnet to the host and port checks basic TCP connectivity. Third, authentication and privileges may prevent access for a given user and host. Finally, resource exhaustion like too many open files or sockets can stop new connections. A concrete example: if systemctl shows the server is active but telnet to port 3306 times out, the network or firewall is likely the cause, not credentials. A common misconception is to assume a permissions problem when the server is down or the port is closed; always confirm the server and network first. Your verification steps: confirm mysqld is running, test TCP connectivity, then check MySQL grants and error log entries for authentication failures. Closing question: when you see a connection error, which of those three checks will you run in what order and why?

The "Too many connections" error (ERROR 1040) indicates the server has reached its configured max_connections limit. This can be a capacity problem or an application issue. Start diagnosis by checking SHOW GLOBAL STATUS LIKE 'Max_used_connections'; to see the peak concurrent connections historically. If Max_used_connections rarely approaches max_connections, then occasional spikes may be transient, and a temporary increase can help while you investigate. Use SHOW PROCESSLIST or sys. processlist to see active connections and identify many sleeping connections or long-running queries. A concrete example: an application that fails to close connections properly will accumulate many sleeping connections until the limit is reached. A common misconception is that raising max_connections always solves the problem; raising it can increase server memory usage and delay discovery of leaks. The correct long-term solution is often application-side: introduce or tune connection pooling so connections are reused and closed promptly. As a diagnostic step, you can SET GLOBAL max_connections = 200 temporarily, but plan to identify and fix the root cause. What would you look for in the process list to decide between a temporary increase and an application fix?

SHOW PROCESSLIST and the sys. processlist view are indispensable for seeing who is connected and what they are doing. Processlist rows show the connection id, user, host, command, time, and Info field with the query text. Start by ordering output by Time to find long-running queries and by Command to find many Sleep entries. A concrete example: SELECT * FROM sys. processlist WHERE command!= 'Sleep' ORDER BY TIME DESC; highlights active queries consuming resources. When you see long-running statements holding connections, examine their query text and EXPLAIN them. Use KILL only for queries you are confident are safe to terminate, and avoid killing transactions mid-write without understanding potential rollback costs. A common misconception is to mass-kill sleeping connections to free slots; sleeping connections often belong to connection pools that will reopen and might mask the leak without fixing the pooling logic. Closing question: when you see many sleeping connections from one host, what is the likely application-level cause and what metric will you monitor after fixing it? Using SHOW PROCESSLIST and sys.processlist means filter by command and time to identify active work and idle connections; kill with care and investigate pooling behavior for many sleeps.. In practical terms, find idle connections, long-running queries, and candidates for kill. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The slow query log records queries that exceed a configured execution time and is central to finding recurring performance problems. Enable slow query logging by setting slow_query_log = 1, long_query_time = 1, and specifying slow_query_log_file in my. cnf, then restart if necessary. With the log enabled, you will capture queries that are candidates for optimization. Tools like mysqldumpslow or pt-query-digest parse the log and surface the most frequent or slowest queries, which helps prioritize work. A concrete example from the hands-on activity: selecting from a large users table without an index on email produces a high execution time entry in the slow log. Use EXPLAIN on that query to see type = ALL and a large rows value; that indicates a full table scan. A common misconception is to assume a single slow query is the only problem; often a family of similar queries will dominate. After identifying the offenders, add targeted indexes or rewrite queries, then monitor the slow log again to confirm improvement. Which query will you check first in your application's slow log? Diagnosing slow queries with the slow query log means enable the slow query log, parse it for frequent offenders, then use explain to prioritize indexing and rewrites.. In practical terms, enable and analyze the slow query log to find frequent offenders. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

EXPLAIN shows how MySQL plans to execute a SELECT, helping you find full table scans and other inefficiencies. Look for type values like ALL, which indicate a full table scan, and Extra values such as Using filesort or Using temporary. The rows column shows the estimated number of rows examined. A concrete walkthrough: run EXPLAIN on a query that searches users by email. If EXPLAIN shows type = ALL and a large rows value, add an index on the email column with CREATE INDEX idx_email ON users (email);. After adding the index, EXPLAIN should change to type = ref or const and rows should be much smaller, and the actual execution time will drop. A misconception is to add indexes without checking selectivity or query patterns; unnecessary or duplicate indexes add write overhead. Always test index impact and prefer composite indexes that match WHERE clause ordering when queries filter by multiple columns. Closing question: after adding an index, which EXPLAIN columns will you inspect to confirm the improvement and why? Using EXPLAIN and adding indexes means use explain to identify scans and rows examined, then add targeted indexes and re-check explain to confirm reduced row estimates and better type values.. In practical terms, interpret query plans and apply indexes to reduce scans. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

To diagnose, inspect the error log for deadlock messages and run SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS\G to view the LATEST DETECTED DEADLOCK section. That output shows the involved transactions, the locks they hold, and the S Q L statements; this is the most informative source for understanding the conflict. A concrete example: two transactions updating rows in two tables in opposite order can deadlock. A practical prevention strategy is to ensure transactions acquire locks in a consistent order, keep transactions short, and add indexes to shorten lock durations. A common misconception is that changing isolation levels always removes deadlocks; while READ COMMITTED can reduce contention compared to REPEATABLE READ, logical ordering and short transactions are more reliable. Your task after seeing deadlocks: read the InnoDB status output to identify the conflicting statements, then change transaction order or index patterns to eliminate the circular wait. What change would you make first if two transactions lock tables in opposite order?

Symptoms include "No space left on device" in the error log, failed writes, and sudden server instability. Start diagnosis with df -h to find the impacted filesystem and du -sh /var/lib/mysql/* to identify large files. Binary logs, slow query logs, error logs, and large. ibd tablespaces are common culprits. A concrete remediation sequence: first, make a backup of essential data and logs. Second, purge old binary logs safely using PURGE BINARY LOGS TO 'mysql-bin.000123'; or set EXPIRE_LOGS_DAYS to limit retention. Third, rotate and compress logs to reclaim space. Fourth, consider OPTIMIZE TABLE table_name when innodb_file_per_table is enabled to free space after deletions, but understand it rebuilds the table and can be resource intensive. A common misconception is to delete files from the data directory directly; doing that can corrupt metadata or replication. Always use MySQL commands or rotate logs in cooperation with the server. Safety is paramount when troubleshooting production databases. Before any structural change, take a recent backup and, when possible, test the change in staging. Keep a copy of my. cnf before editing configuration variables so you can revert. When you need to free space or kill processes, document your actions and reasons so you can trace outcomes. Avoid deleting files directly from the MySQL data directory; use built-in commands to purge or rotate logs. When issuing KILL on threads, understand whether they are inside transactions and whether rollbacks will take time or lock resources. Always prefer making configuration changes with a clear rollback plan and changelog entry. This hands-on activity walks through the chapter lab to reproduce a slow query, analyze it with EXPLAIN, add an index, and confirm improvement. First, create a sample database and a users table without an index on email. Insert a large number of rows to simulate production. Next, run EXPLAIN on the same SELECT and look for type = ALL and a large rows estimate — these indicate a full table scan. Add an index with CREATE INDEX idx_email ON users (email); then re-run EXPLAIN and the SELECT. You should see the type change to ref or const and a dramatic reduction in execution time. A common misconception is to expect any index will help; the index must match the query filter. Always re-run EXPLAIN and check the slow query log to confirm the fix.
